candidates.title: NetConfig-Semantic: A NetOps Benchmark for Semantic Correctness of LLM-Generated Configs
candidates.research_question: Can a publicly reproducible benchmark measuring reachability, ACL semantics, and BGP policy fidelity reliably distinguish semantic correctness of LLM-generated network configurations across varied topologies and vendor syntaxes?
hypotheses: LLM-generated configurations will exhibit substantially higher semantic-error rates (reachability or policy violations) than syntactically-correct baselines when evaluated under realistic control/data-plane models.
A benchmark that reports reachability and ACL-equivalence metrics will expose error modes not visible to token/fluency metrics and will produce stable model rankings across repeated seeds.
candidates.proposed_design: Construct a public dataset of 120 intent→config tasks covering three vendor syntaxes (vendor-A CLI, vendor-B CLI, and a vendor-neutral device model) and three topology classes (edge, datacenter, multi-AS). For each intent task, produce a gold-reference config and an oracle reachable/policy model (using Batfish-style verifier or NetKAT mappings). Query one hosted LLM (standard API) with a fixed prompt template to generate configs (5 seeds per task). Evaluate each generated config with the verifier to compute reachability, ACL-equivalence, BGP policy-preservation, and syntactic-parsing success. Provide tooling, task JSON, verifier input, and all outputs in a public repo.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task, per-seed records: generated config text, parse status, verifier pass/fail flags for reachability/ACL/BGP, violation traces (counterexamples), and metadata (model prompt, seed, timestamp). Aggregated tables of per-task error rates, metric distributions, and model-seed variance.
candidates.primary_outcome: Benchmark utility measured as (a) effect size: difference in verifier-detected semantic-error rate between LLM outputs and gold baselines; and (b) internal consistency: rank-stability of models across bootstrapped task samples.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute per-task semantic-error rates and 95% confidence intervals via bootstrap; compare LLM vs baseline using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; compute Cohen's d for effect sizes; report Kendall tau rank-stability across 1,000 bootstrap resamples; analyze failure traces to classify common semantic error types and correlate with topology/vendor class.
risks: Verifier abstractions may not cover all semantic nuances (lossy mapping) leading to false positives/negatives.
Synthetic dataset may not generalize to production heterogeneity.
Hosted-model API rate limits or outages could interrupt runs.
Dataset construction may inadvertently bias tasks toward verifier-covered properties.

candidates.title: Bounded Repair Loops for Intent→Config: Optimal Iteration Budgets in NetOps Repair
candidates.research_question: For LLM-driven intent→configuration pipelines with verifier feedback, what iteration budget maximizes semantic-correctness gains per model-call cost for typical NetOps tasks?
hypotheses: Most semantic-correctness improvement from iterative generate→validate→repair occurs within the first three repair iterations for NetOps intent→config tasks.
Beyond an empirically determined budget (3–5 iterations), additional iterations yield diminishing returns that are not cost-justified under model-call constraints.
candidates.proposed_design: Use the NetConfig-Semantic dataset subset (60 tasks). Implement a closed-loop pipeline: LLM generates config → verifier checks → provide structured counterexample feedback → LLM repairs, up to 8 iterations or until verifier success. Run with fixed prompts and three random seeds per task. Record per-iteration verifier outcomes, model calls, latency, and final success. Compare fixed budgets (1,3,5,8) on correctness and model-call efficiency.
candidates.expected_data: Iteration-level logs: for each task and seed, iteration number, generated config, verifier pass/fail, counterexample content, cumulative model calls, and final success flag. Aggregated curves of success probability vs iteration and cost-efficiency (success per 100 model calls).
candidates.primary_outcome: Cost-effectiveness curve: semantic-success probability as a function of iteration budget and model-call cost; identification of the budget with maximal marginal gain per model call.
candidates.analysis_outline: Estimate success-probability curves with 95% CIs via bootstrap; compute marginal success increase per additional iteration; apply segmented regression to identify elbow point; perform paired comparisons of budgets (McNemar test on paired success outcomes) and cost-effectiveness ratios with bootstrapped CIs.
risks: Repair prompts may leak verifier internals, biasing results.
Counterexample quality may vary, reducing repair signal effectiveness.
Model API rate limits could force uneven seed execution.
Findings may depend on the particular LLM chosen and not generalize to others.

candidates.title: Verified Agentic NetOps Pipeline: Measuring Safety Gains from Deterministic Verifier Integration
candidates.research_question: Does integrating a deterministic network verifier into an agentic LLM NetOps pipeline measurably reduce deployment-risk actions (unsafe configs) compared to an unverified agentic pipeline under matched task workloads?
hypotheses: An agentic pipeline augmented with a deterministic verifier and fail-safe enforcement will produce significantly fewer unsafe deployment actions than an equivalent pipeline without verification.
Verifier-augmented pipelines will trade reduced unsafe actions for modest increases in human-review flags (false positives), measurable by verifier coverage metrics.
candidates.proposed_design: Implement two agentic pipelines: (A) Agent-only: LLM agent plans and issues configs/actions to a simulated execution queue; (B) Agent+Verifier: same agent but every planned action passes through a deterministic verifier; verifier-failing actions are blocked and routed for auto-repair or human-review flagging. Use 100 multi-step operational tasks (change plans affecting routing and ACLs) in a simulated multi-vendor environment. Measure unsafe deployments (verifier-detected violations that would reach production), blocked unsafe attempts, false-positive flags, and time-to-resolution.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task logs of planned actions, verifier decisions (pass/block), deployments executed, any violations observed post-deployment in control-plane simulation, counts of human-review flags, and latency metrics.
candidates.primary_outcome: Reduction in unsafe deployments (proportion of tasks resulting in unsafe config applied) between Agent-only and Agent+Verifier pipelines; secondary outcome: false-positive flag rate and mean time-to-resolution.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compare proportions of unsafe deployments using two-proportion z-tests with exact binomial CIs; compute relative risk reduction and number-needed-to-block; analyze false-positive rates and latency with Mann–Whitney U tests; report subgroup analyses by vendor-syntax and task type.
risks: Simulator fidelity may under- or over-estimate real deployment risk.
Verifier may block legitimate planned changes (false positives), inflating human-review burden.
Agent implementation variability could confound pipeline comparison if agent behavior diverges across runs.
Integration complexity across synthetic vendor syntaxes may cause mapping errors.

candidates.title: Runtime Monitors for Agentic Tool-Execution Hallucinations in NetOps
candidates.research_question: Can lightweight runtime monitors detect agent tool-execution hallucinations (e.g., false API calls, fabricated device responses, invalid CLI commands) with acceptable false-positive/false-negative rates in LLM-driven NetOps agents?
hypotheses: A runtime-monitor ensemble (syntax checker + API-result plausibility filter + command-execution sandbox) will detect >80% of agent tool-execution hallucinations with a false-positive rate <10% on curated NetOps scenarios.
Detection performance will degrade on adversarially-crafted hallucination variants but remain substantially above random baseline.
candidates.proposed_design: Create a corpus of 600 agent action traces: 300 benign (correct tool calls and plausible responses) and 300 injected hallucinations (fabricated API endpoints, impossible device responses, malformed CLI sequences). Implement runtime monitors: lexical/grammar CLI parser, API-response schema validator, and sandboxed execution comparator. Evaluate detection metrics (TPR, FPR, precision, recall) and test robustness with adversarial perturbations (e.g., paraphrased hallucination messages).
candidates.expected_data: Per-trace monitor outputs, binary detection labels, timestamps, detected-subtype codes, and aggregated ROC curves and precision–recall curves under standard and adversarial conditions.
candidates.primary_outcome: Detection performance summarized as TPR and FPR; primary success threshold: TPR≥0.80 and FPR≤0.10 on held-out test traces.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute ROC and AUC; report point estimates and 95% CIs for TPR and FPR; compare monitor ensemble to single-monitor baselines using McNemar tests; perform error analysis on false negatives to categorize undetected hallucination types.
risks: Constructed hallucination corpus may not reflect real-world hallucination diversity.
Monitors could be evaded by sophisticated adversarial phrasing.
Sandbox comparators may impose performance overhead unsuitable for low-latency operations.
False positives may reduce operator trust and increase alert fatigue.
